Rust in Android Development: Complete Guide

Chayan Mistry
5 min read
·
2 days ago

A step-by-step guide to integrating Rust with Android development using JNI (Java Native Interface). This project demonstrates how to write performance-critical code in Rust and call it from Kotlin/Java in an Android application.
使用 JNI（Java 本地接口）将 Rust 与 Android 开发集成的分步指南。该项目展示了如何在 Rust 中编写性能关键代码，并在 Android 应用程序中从 Kotlin/Java 调用它。

Prerequisites

Before starting, ensure you have:

Required Software

  • Android Studio (latest version)
  • Rust (1.70+): Install from rustup.rs
  • Android NDK (r25 or later): Install via Android Studio’s SDK Manager
  • Cargo (comes with Rust)

Verify Installation

# Check Rust installation
rustc --version
cargo --version

Step-by-Step Setup Guide

Step 1: Create a New Android Project

  1. Open Android Studio
  2. Create a new project with Empty Activity template
  3. Choose Kotlin as the language
  4. Set minimum SDK to API 24 or higher

Step 2: Initialize Rust Project

In your project root directory:

# Create Rust library
cargo init --lib

Step 3: Configure Cargo.toml

Edit Cargo.toml to specify the library type and dependencies:

[package]
name = "rustdemo"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"

[lib]
crate-type = ["cdylib"]  # Compile as C-compatible dynamic library

[dependencies]
jni = "0.21"  # JNI bindings for Rust

[profile.release]
opt-level = 3      # Maximum optimization
lto = true         # Link-time optimization
strip = true       # Strip symbols for smaller binary

Step 4: Build Rust Library for Android

You’ll compile the Rust library directly using Cargo and place the resulting .so files in the Android project’s jiniLibs directory. This is handled through a build script (see the Building the Project section).

Writing Rust Code

Basic Structure

Your src/lib.rs should follow this pattern:

use jni::JNIEnv;
use jni::objects::{JClass, JString};
use jni::sys::jstring;

// ============================================================================
// Core Rust Functions (Pure Business Logic)
// ============================================================================

/// Pure Rust function - no JNI dependencies
pub fn get_hello_string() -> &'static str {
    "Hello from Rust!"
}

/// Pure Rust function with parameters
pub fn greet(name: &str) -> String {
    format!("Hello, {}! Greetings from Rust!", name)
}

// ============================================================================
// JNI Wrappers (Bridge between Java and Rust)
// ============================================================================

/// JNI function callable from Java/Kotlin
#[no_mangle]
pub extern "C" fn Java_com_example_rustdemo_MainActivity_helloFromRust(
    env: JNIEnv,
    _class: JClass,
) -> jstring {
    let message = get_hello_string();
    let output = env
        .new_string(message)
        .expect("Failed to create Java string");
    output.into_raw()
}

/// JNI function with String parameter
#[no_mangle]
pub extern "C" fn Java_com_example_rustdemo_MainActivity_greetFromRust(
    mut env: JNIEnv,
    _class: JClass,
    name: JString,
) -> jstring {
    // Convert Java String to Rust String
    let name_str: String = env
        .get_string(&name)
        .expect("Couldn't get java string!")
        .into();

    // Call core Rust function
    let greeting = greet(&name_str);

    // Convert back to Java String
    let output = env
        .new_string(&greeting)
        .expect("Failed to create Java string!");
    output.into_raw()
}

JNI Function Naming Convention

JNI functions must follow this naming pattern:

Java_<package>_<class>_<method>

Example:

  • Package: com.example.rustdemo
  • Class: MainActivity
  • Method: helloFromRust
  • Full name: Java_com_example_rustdemo_MainActivity_helloFromRust

Best Practices

  1. Separate Logic from JNI: Keep pure Rust functions separate from JNI wrappers
  2. Error Handling: Use .expect() for JNI calls or implement proper error handling
  3. Memory Management: JNI handles memory; use into_raw() to transfer ownership
  4. Type Conversions: Use JNI types for parameters and return values

Building the Project

Create a build script build_rust.sh in your project root:

#!/bin/bash

# Build Rust library for Android
cd "$(dirname "$0")"

# Install cargo-ndk if not already installed
if ! command -v cargo-ndk &> /dev/null; then
    echo "Installing cargo-ndk..."
    cargo install cargo-ndk
fi

# Add Android targets
rustup target add aarch64-linux-android armv7-linux-androideabi x86_64-linux-android i686-linux-android

# Build for all Android targets
echo "Building Rust library for Android..."
cargo ndk -t arm64-v8a -t armeabi-v7a -t x86 -t x86_64 build --release

# Copy libraries to Android project
echo "Copying libraries to Android project..."
mkdir -p app/src/main/jniLibs/arm64-v8a
mkdir -p app/src/main/jniLibs/armeabi-v7a
mkdir -p app/src/main/jniLibs/x86
mkdir -p app/src/main/jniLibs/x86_64

cp target/aarch64-linux-android/release/librustdemo.so app/src/main/jniLibs/arm64-v8a/
cp target/armv7-linux-androideabi/release/librustdemo.so app/src/main/jniLibs/armeabi-v7a/
cp target/i686-linux-android/release/librustdemo.so app/src/main/jniLibs/x86/
cp target/x86_64-linux-android/release/librustdemo.so app/src/main/jniLibs/x86_64/

echo "Build complete!"

Make it executable and run:

chmod +x build_rust.sh
./build_rust.sh

This script:

  1. Installs cargo-ndk if not already installed
  2. Adds Android targets to Rust
  3. Builds the library for all architectures (arm64-v8a, armeabi-v7a, x86, x86_64)
  4. Copies the compiled .so files to the appropriate jniLibs directories

Verify Build Output

After building, verify the .so file exists:

ls -lh app/src/main/jniLibs/arm64-v8a/librustdemo.so

Calling Rust from Kotlin

Step 1: Declare Native Methods

In your Kotlin Activity:

class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    companion object {
        init {
            // Load the Rust library
            System.loadLibrary("rustdemo")
        }
    }

    private lateinit var binding: ActivityMainBinding

    // Declare native methods
    external fun helloFromRust(): String
    external fun greetFromRust(name: String): String

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        binding = ActivityMainBinding.inflate(layoutInflater)
        setContentView(binding.root)

        // Call Rust functions
        val message = helloFromRust()
        val greeting = greetFromRust("Android")

        binding.textView.text = greeting
    }
}

Step 2: Load the Library

The System.loadLibrary() call in the companion object loads the native library when the class is first accessed.

companion object {
    init {
        System.loadLibrary("rustdemo")
    }
}

Step 3: Call the Functions

val result = helloFromRust()  // Returns "Hello from Rust!"
val greeting = greetFromRust("World")  // Returns "Hello, World! Greetings from Rust!"

Testing

Unit Tests for Rust Code

Create src/lib.rs tests:

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn test_get_hello_string() {
        assert_eq!(get_hello_string(), "Hello from Rust!");
    }

    #[test]
    fn test_greet() {
        let result = greet("Alice");
        assert_eq!(result, "Hello, Alice! Greetings from Rust!");
    }
}

Run tests:

cargo test

Android Instrumented Tests

Create app/src/androidTest/java/com/example/rustdemo/RustIntegrationTest.kt

@RunWith(AndroidJUnit4::class)
class RustIntegrationTest {
    @Test
    fun testHelloFromRust() {
        val activity = MainActivity()
        val result = activity.helloFromRust()
        assert(result.contains("Rust"))
    }
}

Performance Considerations

1. Minimize JNI Calls

JNI calls have overhead. Batch operations when possible:

// ❌ Inefficient: Multiple JNI calls
for (i in 0..1000) {
    processItem(i)  // JNI call
}

// ✅ Efficient: Single JNI call with batch processing
processBatch(items)  // Single JNI call

2. Use Appropriate Data Types

// ❌ Inefficient: String conversion overhead
pub fn process_string(s: String) -> String { }

// ✅ Efficient: Use references when possible
pub fn process_string(s: &str) -> String { }

3. Profile Your Code

Use Android Profiler to identify bottlenecks:

  1. Run → Profile
  2. Select CPU profiler
  3. Look for JNI overhead

4. Optimize Rust Build

[profile.release]
opt-level = 3      # Maximum optimization
lto = true         # Link-time optimization
codegen-units = 1  # Better optimization (slower build)
strip = true       # Smaller binary
